mcq.q: Registration of a partnership firm under the Partnership Act, 1932 is:
options: Compulsory within 30 days of formation
Optional, and may be done at any time, but non-registration brings disabilities under Section 69
Compulsory before starting business
Not possible after the firm starts business
mcq.explain: The Act does not make registration compulsory, and a firm may apply for registration at any time by filing a statement under Section 58. However, Section 69 imposes serious disabilities on unregistered firms, such as being unable to sue third parties on contracts, so registration is advisable.
mcq.fast: Registration: optional + any time; consequence of not registering = s.69.

mcq.q: An unregistered firm files a suit against a customer to recover ₹2,50,000 for goods supplied. The suit is:
options: Not maintainable — Section 69(2)
Maintainable
Maintainable if the firm registers during the suit
Maintainable if the amount is below ₹5 lakh
mcq.explain: Section 69(2) stops an unregistered firm from suing an outsider to enforce a contractual right. Registration must exist on the date the suit is filed; registering later does not cure the defect. The amount involved does not matter, except for the separate ₹100 rule on set-offs.
mcq.fast: Unregistered firm cannot SUE outsiders on contracts; it can still BE SUED.

mcq.q: Which suit is allowed even though the firm is unregistered?
options: A suit by a partner for dissolution of the firm and for accounts
A suit by the firm against a debtor for ₹50,000
A suit by a partner against another partner to enforce a right under the deed, while the firm continues
A claim of set-off by the firm for ₹10,000
mcq.explain: Section 69(3) saves a partner's right to sue for dissolution of the firm, for accounts of a dissolved firm, or to realise the property of a dissolved firm. It also saves claims of set-off or suits not exceeding ₹100 in value. Suits by the firm against outsiders, or between partners of a continuing unregistered firm, are barred.
mcq.fast: Allowed = dissolution, accounts, realising property, claims ≤ ₹100.

mcq.q: A firm of three partners is dissolved compulsorily under Section 41 when:
options: One partner falls ill for a month
Two of the three partners are adjudged insolvent
The firm makes a loss in one year
A partner wants to retire
mcq.explain: Section 41 provides for compulsory dissolution when all the partners or all but one are adjudged insolvent, or when an event makes it unlawful to carry on the business. With two of three partners insolvent, only one is left solvent, so the firm stands dissolved. A temporary illness or a single loss year are not grounds.
mcq.topic: Dissolution of a firm and its modes (Sections 39 to 43)
mcq.fast: Compulsory: all/all-but-one insolvent, or business unlawful.

mcq.q: Which is NOT a ground on which a court may dissolve a firm under Section 44?
options: A partner has become of unsound mind
The business can only be carried on at a loss
A partner persistently commits breach of the partnership agreement
A partner is adjudged insolvent
mcq.explain: Section 44 lets the court dissolve a firm on grounds such as a partner's unsound mind, permanent incapacity, misconduct, persistent breach of agreement, transfer of his whole interest, business possible only at a loss, or any just and equitable reason. Insolvency of a partner is dealt with under Section 42, as a contingency that dissolves the firm, subject to contract.
mcq.fast: Insolvency = s.42 (contingency), not a court ground under s.44.

mcq.q: On dissolution, a firm's assets realise ₹5,00,000. Outside creditors are owed ₹3,00,000 and partner A has given a loan of ₹50,000 to the firm. How much is available to repay partners' capital?
mcq.explain: Section 48 applies the assets in this order: first the firm's debts to third parties, then advances by partners (as distinct from capital), then partners' capital, and finally any surplus in the profit-sharing ratio. ₹5,00,000 − ₹3,00,000 − ₹50,000 = ₹1,50,000 is left for capital.
mcq.topic: Settlement of accounts (Section 48) and firm vs separate debts (Section 49)
mcq.fast: Order: outsiders -> partners' loans -> capital -> surplus.

mcq.q: After dissolution, partners remain liable to third parties for acts done by any of them that would have been acts of the firm if done before dissolution, until:
options: The assets are sold
Public notice of the dissolution is given — Section 45
The bank account is closed
The Registrar cancels the registration
mcq.explain: Section 45 continues the partners' liability to third parties for acts done by any of them after dissolution which would have bound the firm before it, until public notice of the dissolution is given. The estate of a deceased partner, an insolvent partner, or a dormant partner who was not known to the third party is not liable.
mcq.topic: Liability, winding-up rights and continuing authority after dissolution (Sections 45 to 47)
mcq.fast: Same rule as retirement: liability till public notice.

mcq.q: A partnership at will can be dissolved by:
options: Only the court
Only the majority of partners
Any one partner, by a written notice of dissolution sent to every other partner — Section 43
Only the Registrar of Firms
mcq.explain: Section 43 lets any one partner end a partnership at will by a written notice sent to every other partner. Dissolution takes effect on the date the notice names, or, failing that, on the day the notice reaches the partners.
mcq.topic: Dissolution of a firm and its modes (Sections 39 to 43)
mcq.fast: At will = one partner, one written notice.

mcq.q: In settling accounts on dissolution, losses including deficiency of capital are paid first out of:
options: Partners' private property first
Profits, then capital, and lastly by partners individually in the profit-sharing ratio — Section 48(a)
Capital first, then profits
Outside creditors' claims
mcq.explain: Section 48(a) sets the order for meeting losses, including a capital shortfall: profits first, capital next, and finally the partners' own pockets in their profit-sharing ratio. Only after that are the assets distributed under Section 48(b).
mcq.topic: Settlement of accounts (Section 48) and firm vs separate debts (Section 49)
